scenarios.outcome: Recorded 2026-08-28 by wave 4, whole. The pinned passcode derives the pinned controller prefix EB3UGWwIMq7ppzcQ697ImQIuXlBG5jzh-baSx-YG3-tY against a live agent — the reference passes 24 characters and silently derives from the first 21, so the recording carries both spellings and the truncation is explicit. The witnessed identifier's agent and witness OOBIs match the upstream case's local-branch literals exactly, and two further clients cross-resolve each other's agent OOBIs, each resolution answering with the other's prefix. Two findings: the deployment serves six introduction URLs where upstream's `validate config` deep-equals exactly three, so the reference's own assertion would refuse the deployment its suite targets; and the first witnessed record broke the port's decoder — `windexes` arrives as JSON numbers where the reference's schema declares strings — now widened to `WitnessIndex`.
scenarios.note: Boot and connect one client and two, derive a controller prefix from a pinned passcode, and cross-resolve agent OOBIs as contacts.

scenarios.outcome: Recorded 2026-08-28 by wave 5, whole. An unwitnessed identifier starts with zero agent-role authorisations, gains exactly one on the grant ({cid, agent, agent prefix}), grants the mailbox role to itself ({cid, mailbox, cid}), and after the location scheme the agent derives the OOBI the upstream case pins — the authorised URL joined to /oobi/{cid}/mailbox/{cid}, the identifier appearing twice because the mailbox is self-controlled. One mapping documented: upstream's helper raw-fetches /identifiers/{alias}/endroles/{role} (the reference SDK exposes no such read), while the port reads the same authorisations by AID through /endroles/{aid}/{role}, and the transcript pins which address answered.
scenarios.note: Authorise the agent role and a self-controlled mailbox, then read back the location scheme the OOBI derives. Needs no witnesses.

scenarios.outcome: Recorded 2026-08-28 by wave 7, whole. The witness's controller OOBI resolves, then four establishment events run at sequences zero to three — incept with Wan at threshold one, rotate keeping it, cut it, add it back — each completing only once the named witness set receipted it, with the key state's witness list evolving [Wan], [Wan], [], [Wan] and the threshold 1, 1, 0, 1 exactly as the upstream case asserts. One finding pinned live: bt changes JSON type with its value inside this single log — text "1" on the inception, bare number 1 on the non-zero rotations, text "0" at zero — which is the multisig rotation's finding reproduced deliberately by this port's event builders, and a real KERIA accepts all four spellings interleaved. Every event's bytes appear verbatim in a successful POST, and every SAID re-verifies hermetically.
scenarios.note: Incept with one witness, rotate, cut the witness, and add it back — the only scenario that exercises a witness receipt end to end.

scenarios.outcome: Recorded 2026-08-28 against the local preset, whole: three creations, the listing ladder with both paged windows, the rotation, the interaction, the key state, the three-event log, the rename, and the operations postcondition. Sixteen of the eighteen pinned qb64 values reproduce exactly — both prefixes, all four keys, all four next-key digests, both thresholds, and the rotation SAID — with the port's exact bytes accepted verbatim by the agent. The two that do not are one decision seen twice: the upstream interaction anchors the bare string [icp.pre], which the port's Vec<Sad> anchors cannot spell, so the recording anchors a seal of the same inception and the interaction SAID and the state digest repeating it differ by design, with both values recorded.
scenarios.note: The richest golden vectors in the suite: eighteen pinned qb64 values from fixed passcodes, plus paging and rename. Needs KERIA alone.

scenarios.outcome: Recorded 2026-08-28 by wave 6, whole. A fresh-entropy identifier incepts, interacts, and rotates against a live agent, the log growing 2 then 3 with every operation waited out and deleted. The decisive check is the key commitment, recomputed hermetically from the recorded events: BLAKE3-256 over the rotation's revealed signing key equals the digest the inception committed to, so a randy rotation rotates to exactly the committed key — and each derived event appears verbatim inside a successful POST body, so the agent accepted the port's own bytes. The interaction anchors a seal of the inception where upstream anchors the bare string [icp.pre], the same Vec<Sad> narrowing wave 3 records.
scenarios.note: Randy inception, interaction, and rotation, with key-event log lengths. Structural only — a randy key is fresh entropy, so nothing can be pinned.

scenarios.outcome: Both halves recorded 2026-08-28. Wave 3 recorded the salty.test.ts half: four pinned identifier inceptions (one single-key, one three-key at threshold two) derived by the port and accepted byte-for-byte by a live agent. Wave 4 recorded the test-setup-single-client.test.ts half: the pinned client passcode deriving the pinned controller prefix, and witnessed inceptions with the environment's whole triple at threshold three, receipted by the running witnesses.
scenarios.note: A pinned passcode deriving a pinned controller prefix, which is the one place a live run can confirm the port's derivation against a real agent's.

scenarios.outcome: Recorded 2026-08-28 by wave 8. A witnessed identifier rotates; the owner's key state moves at once — sequence incremented, both key fields changed — while the observing client's stays one sequence behind until it refreshes with keyStates().query at the new sequence, spelled in hexadecimal (wave 1's answer), after which the remote state carries exactly the new signing key and commitment. The query's exact sequence text is proven sent from the observer's transcript, the rotation's SAID re-verifies over the derived bytes, and both clients end with zero operations listed.
scenarios.note: Rotation, and the local-versus-remote key-state divergence a second client sees until it refreshes.

scenarios.outcome: Recorded 2026-08-28 by wave 8, as the rotation's twin: the interaction increments the sequence while changing no keys, the observer is one behind until the hexadecimal refresh, and — unlike the bare-string anchors of waves 3 and 6 — upstream's own anchor here is the empty object, which a Sad can spell, so the event reproduces upstream exactly with "a": [{}].
scenarios.note: An interaction event and the same divergence, one sequence number behind.

scenarios.outcome: Recorded 2026-08-29 by wave 10, both files whole. Two delegated inceptions — one unwitnessed, one witnessed by the whole triple at threshold three — and a delegated rotation, every establishment pending under its delegation.{said} operation until the delegator anchored its seal with a plain interaction (byte-identical to wave 9's delegation-address approval but for the path, which is the delegation approval's finding used in the other direction). The delegate's agent saw the first anchor through a sequence query and the second through an anchor query, whose idempotence the upstream case asserts and this recording repeats. The drt is itself a delegated event, completing as t=drt at s=1. The wave found the port's third live-only defect: the agent echoes an anchor query's seal back in the caller's own {i,s,d} shape with no sn at all, so QueryMetadata's required sn and Anchor-typed anchor refused the first anchor-query answer ever received — widened to Option<EchoedSequence> and EchoedAnchor.
scenarios.note: A delegator anchoring a delegate's inception and then its rotation, with and without witnesses.

scenarios.outcome: Recorded 2026-08-29 by wave 9, whole. A delegated inception's operation is proven pending before approval — the identifier does not exist until the delegator anchors a seal of it — then the approving interaction (built through InceptionSeal, whose fields cannot disagree, where upstream hand-assembles the anchor and reads the delegate's prefix out of an operation name) lands at the delegation address, the delegate's key-state query at sequence one lets its agent see the anchor, and the creation completes with the artifact's own prefix. The tail reproduces upstream's odd contact resolution: the delegate's agent OOBI truncated at /agent/ still resolves and answers the delegate's prefix. One operational fact recorded: a delegation approval spawns a witness operation inside its own metadata.depends, so the zero-operations postcondition requires the dependency walk upstream's deleteOperations performs.
scenarios.note: The single-signature approval round. Its port records that this half needs two connected clients and a live agent.

scenarios.outcome: Wave 13 recorded multisig-inception.test.ts whole: witnessed (threshold two) and witnessless groups, both members deriving the same prefix each time, with the witnessless members listing — which upstream dare not assert against keria#189 — answering correctly on this deployment. Wave 14 recorded multisig-join.test.ts's spine: a 1-of-1 group, a rotation committing a third member into rotation authority (two signers, three commitments), then a second rotation he joins by REBUILDING it from the proposal's member lists and his own queried key states — composing the group keeper from KeeperRequest::Group with the prior event's commitments and driving rotate_identifier over the group's queried prior state — comparing the SAID he built with the SAID he was shown before groups().join submits his signature; the SAIDs agree and he seats into a three-key signing set. Two compositions taught the port's shapes: the keeper's next_states are the PRIOR commitments a rotation signature indexes into, and the port's rotation announcement reaches the signing peers, so a rotation-authority-only member is not told — upstream tells him by hand through its free-form recipient list, and he needs nothing from that message. **Still to do:** the four-client member-replacement case under a 3-of-3 threshold at the join file's tail.
scenarios.note: Group inception with and without witnesses, then adding a third member by rotation and joining. Gives `sendRequest` and `join` their first consumers.

Upstream carries this only inside `multisig.test.ts`, which needs vLEI for its credential tail. The rounds themselves need no credentials, so this port should drive them in a scenario of its own rather than inherit that coupling.
Both sides of a delegation as groups. Its port records that the round is not driven end to end because it needs four connected clients.
The GLEIF chain — GLEIF to QVI to LE to ECR and OOR — across six schemas.
The same chain with every party a group: nine clients, the largest scenario in the suite.

The most complete IPEX matrix: registry, issue, grant/admit, the apply-offer-agree-grant-admit presentation, a chained credential, revoke, and delete. The scenario now exists as `wave15_credential_ipex`, and its two schemas (QVI and LE) are served by the deployment's schema source, so this row is no longer blocked on infrastructure — only on a recording run.

A group acting as credential holder, admitting a grant from a single-signature issuer over `/multisig/exn`. The scenario exists as `wave16_multisig_credentials` and the QVI schema it needs is served. Driven four times on 2026-09-16 to record the correction of the joining member's peer resolution (the decision that group IPEX announcements carry member lists): it now runs through the group's registry and issuance rounds and stops on four live-only decode defects ahead of the grant and admit — an integer anchor-seal sequence in the credential state, a registry operation without `pre`, the schema OOBI's operation shape, and a read credential that does not re-serialize to its SAID — each an open question. Blocked on those, not on infrastructure.

scenarios.outcome: Recorded 2026-08-29 by wave 11, whole. Both generations answer BIP39's own arithmetic — twelve words at 128 bits, twenty-four at 256, through ChallengeStrength's closed set where upstream stringifies any number. Bob's response travels as an exchange message on /challenge/response, and the message Alice's verification answers with is the very one Bob sent, tied by SAID across two clients; after the acknowledgement, Bob's contact carries the twelve words authenticated and naming that SAID. One operational fact recorded: the respond submission's operation is born done — wave 2's finding — yet stays listed until deleted, and upstream's own case never waits its respond, which would leave its assertOperations one message behind.
scenarios.note: Two clients exchange challenge words, sign them back, verify, and mark the response accepted. **This row did not exist in the scenario table**: the audit found `challenge.test.ts` claimed by no scenario row, so the table omitted a whole capability. This audit adds it.

scenarios.outcome: Recorded 2026-08-29 by wave 12, whole — and the first live drive of the port's multisig machinery: a two-member witnessed group incepted through propose_inception/accept_inception with both members deriving the same prefix, then the group end-role round expressed through public API alone (add_end_role on the group alias signing with the member's indexed key, the reply travelling as an rpy embed under the group's establishment seal on /multisig/rpy, one shared stamp so both members derive the same reply SAID — the group IPEX rounds' one-clock lesson applied). Alice, a third party, resolves the group's truncated OOBI and asks five questions: the group's roles name exactly both agents (all cid the group, all role agent), the agent filter answers the same set, a role nobody granted and a well-formed identifier nobody owns answer empty rather than erroring, and her own identifier answers exactly her agent. One wire fact recorded: the rpy relay must carry the {gid} payload — without it, no /multisig/rpy notification is ever raised, which is how the first run stalled.
scenarios.note: A third party reading the end roles of a group it is not a member of.

Registering an external key manager and incepting under `Algos.extern`. **Blocked on this port, not on infrastructure:** `ConnectedClient::keepers()` lends the factory immutably and `KeeperFactory::with_module` consumes `self`, so an external module cannot be registered on a client at all. `signify-client` never names `ExternalKeeperModule`. Owned by the API consistency review.

open_questions.experiment: Record the deployment's identity to the six-element deployment-identity standard. On `docker` that is the image digest, the compose file's hash, the witness configuration, the schema source, the environment variables, the startup command, and the timeout policy. On `localhost` there is no image, so the strongest available identity is the agent's own OpenAPI document, captured verbatim with its SHA-256.
open_questions.outcome: Recorded for the `local` preset: `spec_digest`, version 1.0.1, three witnesses observed serving the expected prefixes, and the six deployment-identity elements. **Not closed** — the row asks for an image digest, which a localhost deployment has none of.
open_questions.note: A localhost run yields observations but not a pin: the row's own text asks for an image digest. The audit test must therefore refuse to let a localhost run close this row. Already in hand: the live agent serves `info.version: 1.0.1`, OpenAPI 3.1.0 — which also corrects the `KERIA OpenAPI source revision/generator` record, whose text says the document 'carries no version'. It does; the version sits at line 2237 of 2240, where a reader checking the head would miss it.

open_questions.experiment: Six observations at least: `identifiers().list` and `notifications().list`, each on an empty page, a partial page, and a complete one, recording the literal header bytes and the status. Then two the reference never tries — a range past the end of the collection, and one whose start exceeds its end — because that is where an unknown total spelled `*` would surface if anywhere.
open_questions.outcome: **Closed.** Five values captured across both endpoints. Every one parses; none spells its total `*`, so the grammar needs no widening — and the decision not to enforce RFC 9110 is vindicated, because asked past the end of a collection KERIA answers `aids 100-0/4`, start greater than end. A parser that had imposed the rule would refuse a response a deployment genuinely sends. A second finding came free: on an empty collection `/identifiers` answers `aids 0-0/1` with status 206 while `/notifications` answers `notes 0-0/0` with status 200.
open_questions.note: Every captured literal is fed through `ContentRange::parse` in a hermetic test, so the answer is checked on every change rather than having been checked once. This port also cannot *send* the inverted range it parses the answer to: `ItemRange::new` refuses `start > end`.

open_questions.due: key events and key states endpoints → integration matrix
open_questions.experiment: Build a log of eleven events (sequence 0 through 10, hexadecimal 0x0 through 0xa) by rotating an identifier ten times, then query sequence ten spelled `"10"` and spelled `"a"`, and record which returns the event actually asked for. Query a **remote** prefix — a second client's identifier resolved by OOBI — because querying your own may be answered from the agent's local key event log without the mailbox query happening at all, which would make the experiment vacuous.
open_questions.outcome: **Closed: hexadecimal.** One client built an eleven-event log and a second, which had learned the prefix through an OOBI, asked about event ten both ways. `a` resolved and returned the key state for event ten; `10` and `16` never resolved, each running until the 30-second deadline — read in base sixteen they name events 16 and 22, which that log does not have. So this deployment reads the query's `sn` in base sixteen, and a caller who spells event ten `"10"` waits until the deadline rather than getting an error. `QuerySequence` keeps both variants and no default: one deployment is evidence about that deployment, and keripy's base-ten reader is still in the tree. **The run also found a port defect**: `QueryMetadata.sn` was `u64` on the reference schema's authority, but KERIA echoes the request's `sn` back verbatim as the string it was sent, so every live query answer failed to decode — including the successful one. Widened to `EchoedSequence`.
open_questions.note: Whatever the answer, both `QuerySequence` variants stay: one deployment does not justify a default, and adding one would undo the argument for having none. The evidence changes the documentation and adds a recommendation at the call site; a default would need a decision of its own.

open_questions.topic: The exchange submission's answer has two declared types
open_questions.experiment: Post one exchange to `/identifiers/{name}/exchanges` and one to `/identifiers/{name}/ipex/{route}`, record both answers verbatim, and run each recorded body through `SentExchange::operation()` and `SentExchange::exchange()`. The two shapes are already proven disjoint, so exactly one decoder must succeed per body; the ledger records which, and whether the two paths agree.
open_questions.outcome: **Closed: both paths answer with an `ExchangeOperation`.** One exchange was posted to `/identifiers/{name}/exchanges` and one apply to `/identifiers/{name}/ipex/apply`, and **both** decoders were run over **both** answers rather than stopping at the first success. Both bodies decode as an operation and neither as an exchange message — `{"name": "exchange.EDOG…", "metadata": {"said": "EDOG…"}, "done": true, "response": {"said": "EDOG…"}}` — which is exactly `Operation<ExchangeMetadata, ExchangeMetadata>`. So `Exchanges.sendFromEvents`'s declared `Promise<Exn>` is **wrong**, and `Ipex.submit*`'s `Promise<ExchangeOperation>` is right. A port that had believed either declaration in isolation had even odds of typing a caller's answer as something it is not. `SentExchange` keeps the body and both decoders, so nothing needs to change; what changes is that `exchange()` is now known never to have succeeded against a deployment.
open_questions.note: The `/exchanges` half is reachable today through `Challenges::respond`, which is recorded as a wrapper over `Exchanges::send` and needs two clients and no vLEI. The ipex half likely needs a schema, so it waits on the vLEI container. **Observed 2026-08-28.** The ipex half did not need the vLEI container after all: an apply names a schema SAID but does not require it to be resolvable, and it carries neither an attachment nor an embedded credential.

open_questions.due: shared API data types → integration matrix
open_questions.experiment: Capture `GET /spec.yaml` verbatim and diff its `required` arrays against the 150 schemas pinned in `fixtures/types-keria-api/v1.json`, recording every field the port requires that the deployment does not send, and every field the deployment declares required that the port treats as optional.
open_questions.outcome: The document is captured and **it carries a version**: `info.version: 1.0.1`, OpenAPI 3.1.0, at line 2239 of a 72,450-byte file — which corrects the row's claim that it 'carries no version'. The `required`-array diff against the 150 pinned schemas is still to do. **Second live reading, 2026-08-28:** the served document has **no `components:` section at all** — its only top-level blocks are `paths` and `info` — so the 150 named schemas the reference's `keria-api-schema.ts` indexes out of `components['schemas'][…]` cannot have been generated from what this deployment serves. The document does declare 127 `required:` arrays, all inline under `paths`, so the diff the residual asks for is still possible but is against inline request and response bodies rather than against named schemas. Recorded in `environment.json` as `spec_sections`, `spec_required_arrays`, and `spec_defines_components`. The residual stays open, now with a known shape.
open_questions.note: The OpenAPI source question is resolved but left this residual explicitly. Capturing the document also gives a localhost deployment its only reproducible identity, recorded in `environment.json` with its digest.

obligations.record: Credential domain types and SAID construction
obligations.claim: The credential bounds are far above anything the pinned tree produces — its largest credential has three attribute fields and two levels — but a real deployment issuing something larger would be refused here and accepted upstream; the integration matrix should confirm them against a live KERIA.
obligations.note: No deployment confirms a bound. A live run can only show KERIA accepting something larger than this port allows, which is a resource-limit question rather than a parity one — alongside the two open questions already owed to the fuzz and security review.

obligations.claim: A freshness window too tight turns a working deployment into one that refuses its own agent; what a real deployment's skew actually is belongs to the integration matrix, and until then a caller whose agent is further out must widen it or switch it off.
obligations.note: A loopback run measures approximately zero skew, which says nothing about deployments in general. What a run can do is record the observed spread of `Signify-Timestamp` against local time and confirm the default window is not too tight **for the pinned deployment**. The row may make that narrowed claim and no more.

obligations.claim: What is proven about the tokio clock is that it compiles and satisfies the trait; that it sleeps for the right duration belongs to the integration matrix.
obligations.note: The claim is that `TokioClock::sleep` delegates to `tokio::time::sleep`. A paused-time tokio test proves that deterministically; asserting real elapsed time against a live agent is flakier and proves less, and any upper bound would make the test depend on the wall clock, which tests here must not.

obligations.claim: `ContentRange` cross-field consistency is not checked, because KERIA's unit is not `bytes` and no evidence here establishes it follows RFC 9110's ordering — inventing the constraint could reject a valid response, and confirming it is the integration matrix's.

obligations.note: Collected here by the maintainer decision of 2026-08-28 so it is tracked rather than buried in prose; the scenario that settles it is named when its wave is recorded. **Settled 2026-08-28 by the `content_range` observation.** No recorded value spells its total `*`, and every one parses — but the deployment does send a start greater than its end (`aids 100-0/4`), which is the stricter grammar's failure mode rather than the unknown total this row anticipated.

obligations.claim: A loopback TLS test would need a certificate authority of its own, so what the tests prove is that the stack is wired and that plaintext can be refused; verifying a real handshake belongs to the integration matrix.
obligations.note: KERIA listens on `127.0.0.1:3901` over **plain HTTP**, so a live run exercises no TLS whatsoever. A row claiming the integration matrix closes this would be false. The record itself notes a loopback test would need a certificate authority of its own — which is one dev-dependency, and proves more than a live run could.
